newsitem.title: GERMANY: German committee rejects government tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German committee rejects government tax reform.

text.p: Germany's parliamentary mediation committee decided early on Thursday to reject government legislation to cut business and corporate taxation by 30 billion marks.

Negotiators from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) did, however, manage after 15 hours of talks to settle a two-year row by agreeing to abolish a capital trading tax on companies.

Formal rejection of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax reforms by the opposition majority on the mediation committee -- a forum for clearing legislative deadlock between the lower house of parliament and the SPD-led higher chamber -- had been expected after preliminary talks found no basis for a deal.
But, committee officials said, the two sides did put together a deal to abolish the capital trading tax next year, thus averting its automatic introduction in depressed eastern Germany.

Rejection of the government's main tax reform, designed to boost investment and cut record post-war unemployment, will send the package back to the Bundestag lower houes, which will hold an emergency session next Tuesday.

The government can then try to force another round of parliamentary mediation, but both sides admit that their differences are too great to find a tax reform compromise before next year's general elections.
